description: Cryocore Horizon is a six-member team from Dhaka, Bangladesh, combining AI, software development, research, data analysis, and visual storytelling. Our project, SAR Atlas, explores flooding, riverbank erosion, and wetland change through interactive maps and radar explainers inspired by NASA’s NISAR mission. We aim to make Earth observation accessible and meaningful. Six minds. One horizon.
summary: SAR Atlas helps people in Chattogram, Bangladesh decide where to check first after monsoon flooding, when clouds hide the ground from ordinary satellite cameras. It compares two calibrated NISAR radar passes over the Karnaphuli river and port, maps where the radar echo changed, and explains each change in plain English or Bangla with a suggested next step. Farmers, agriculture officers and relief teams can tap the map, ask questions, and download a brief with the dates, measurements and NASA sources behind every answer.
details:
Project Details

SAR Atlas: see the flood through the cloud, and know where to check first.

Every monsoon, floods hit Chattogram, Bangladesh. Roads go under, crops are lost and schools close. The worst flooding comes under thick cloud, so optical satellites see nothing. NASA–ISRO NISAR radar sees through cloud, day or night. But radar data is hard to read for the people who need it most: relief planners, local officials, farmers and families.

SAR Atlas turns NISAR radar into a short list of places to check first after a flood. It’s a web app built around a real case study of the Karnaphuli river and Chattogram during the 2026 monsoon.

What it does

  • Through the clouds: a cloudy MODIS photo and NISAR radar from the same morning, side by side. The camera sees white; the radar shows the river, port and fields.
  • Monsoon time-lapse: every radar pass in order, so you can watch water spread over low fields in the wettest week and pull back in the driest.
  • Compare dates: any two passes on synced maps. It checks they were taken the same way, so the change is fair to compare.
  • Calibrated radar (HH / HV): reads every pixel in decibels. Switch between polarizations and tap a pixel to read both values.
  • 3D change map: places where the radar echo changed rise as columns, coloured by their likely cause.
  • Impact & priorities: ranks every union and ward by NISAR’s flood signal, weighed against roads, facilities and cropland. Each comes with a suggested next step, and the list can be downloaded.
  • My Area: answers one question for residents: how is my ward doing? It shows the flooded share seen by radar, the week’s rain, the forecast and where to get help.
  • Ask the map: a plain-language assistant in English or Bangla. It reads the case data, flies the map to the place it means and ends with a place to visit, not a verdict.
  • Evidence & brief: every answer keeps its dates, measurements and NASA sources, and can be saved as an observation brief (CSV) to hand on.

Benefits and intended impact. Responders can prioritise field checks within days of a radar pass instead of waiting for clear skies. Residents get a plain answer about their own area. Because NISAR revisits every 12 days, the same method can scale to any flood-prone river delta it passes over.

How it works and what we used

  • NASA data: NISAR L2 GCOV radar (NASA–ISRO, via the ASF DAAC); NASA Earthdata CMR for scene search; NASA GIBS imagery (MODIS Terra, Blue Marble, VIIRS Black Marble); NASA POWER daily rainfall.
  • Radar processing: Python, FastAPI, SQLite, h5py, rasterio and NumPy. Calibration to decibels, alignment, change detection and region summaries.
  • App: Next.js, React, Mapbox GL and Three.js.
  • Assistant and voice: Google Gemini and ElevenLabs.

How it is creative. Most flood tools stop at a raster map. SAR Atlas turns calibrated radar into ranked places, plain answers and evidence a person can act on.

Factors we considered.

  • Honesty about limits: radar can’t say what happened, only where the echo changed. So the app says “check here”, not “this is flooded”, and shows its measurements, sources and caveats.
  • Fair comparisons: only passes taken the same way are compared.
  • Access: plain language, Bangla support and a resident-focused view.
  • Reproducibility: every figure traces back to open NASA data.
  • Disclaimer: SAR Atlas is not an official NASA or ISRO product.

Team CryoCore Horizon: Alif (Data analyst and Backend Engineer), Abbas (Frontend Engineer), Jahidul (Full-stack Engineer), Mantaka (Visualization & VFX artist), Nusrat (Researcher), Aiman (Narrative)

Use of Super Intelligence (SI): statement

Video footage: The clay-animation intro scenes in our submission video (Chattogram streets, team portraits, Rahim and Mina) were generated with AI video/image tools - Google Flow.

Audio: All narration was generated with ElevenLabs text-to-speech, from scripts written by our team.

Video editing: The final videos were assembled, timed and captioned with an AI coding assistant (Claude Code) driving the HyperFrames HTML-to-video framework. The app footage is real screen recordings of SAR Atlas.

In the app: The “Ask the map” assistant uses Google Gemini to answer questions about the case data.

Code: Parts of the code were written with AI coding assistants and reviewed by our team.

No SI-generated content uses, contains or modifies NASA logos, flags or mission identifiers.
